title: Practice: Pollination and Fertilisation in Plants

questions.stem: A student states: 'Pollination is the same as fertilisation in plants.' Why is this statement incorrect?

options.text: Pollination only happens in wind-pollinated plants, not insect-pollinated ones
Pollination is the transfer of pollen to the stigma; fertilisation is the fusion of the male and female gamete nuclei, which occurs later after the pollen tube grows
Pollination involves seed dispersal, while fertilisation involves pollen transfer
They are the same process but happen at different times of year

questions.explanation: Pollination and fertilisation are two separate events. Pollination is the transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma. After pollination, a pollen tube grows down through the style to the ovule in the ovary. Fertilisation occurs when the male gamete nucleus from the pollen grain travels down the tube and fuses with the female gamete nucleus in the ovule.

questions.stem: After a pollen grain lands on a compatible stigma, it germinates and grows a pollen tube. What provides the energy for pollen tube growth, and what does the tube contain?

options.text: Energy comes from photosynthesis in the pollen grain; the tube contains chloroplasts
Energy comes from nutrients in the style; the tube contains the female gamete
Energy comes from nutrients in the pollen grain; the tube carries the male gamete nucleus to the ovule
Energy comes from water absorbed through the stigma; the tube contains the seed

questions.explanation: The pollen grain contains food reserves that provide energy for the pollen tube to grow down through the style. The tube carries the male gamete nucleus towards the ovule. Enzymes at the tip of the pollen tube digest the tissues of the style, creating a pathway. When the tube reaches the ovule, the male nucleus is released for fertilisation.

questions.stem: A gardener notices that their apple tree flowers abundantly each spring but produces very few apples. The garden has very few insects. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The tree is not getting enough water to produce fruit
Without sufficient insect pollinators, most flowers are not being pollinated, so fertilisation cannot occur and few fruits develop
The flowers are being blown off by wind before they can produce fruit
Apple trees only produce fruit every other year

questions.explanation: Apple trees are insect-pollinated. Without enough insects to transfer pollen between flowers, pollination rates are low. Without pollination, the pollen tube cannot form, fertilisation cannot occur, and the ovules do not develop into seeds. Without fertilised ovules, the ovary does not develop into a fruit (apple).

questions.stem: Cross-pollination produces offspring with more genetic variation than self-pollination. Which of the following correctly explains why?

options.text: Cross-pollination involves pollen from a different plant, so the gametes carry different combinations of alleles
Cross-pollination produces more seeds than self-pollination
Self-pollination involves wind, which damages the pollen DNA
Cross-pollinated seeds germinate faster, giving them more time to develop variation

questions.explanation: In cross-pollination, pollen comes from a genetically different plant, meaning the male gamete carries a different set of alleles from the female gamete. This increases genetic variation in the offspring. In self-pollination, both gametes come from the same plant, so there is less mixing of alleles and offspring are more genetically similar.

questions.stem: A researcher places pollen from Species A onto the stigma of Species B. The pollen grains land on the stigma but no pollen tubes grow. What does this suggest?

options.text: The pollen was too old to germinate
The stigma of Species B does not have the right chemical signals to stimulate pollen tube growth from Species A pollen, preventing cross-species fertilisation
Species B is wind-pollinated, so it rejects all insect-carried pollen
The pollen grains were damaged during transfer

questions.explanation: Stigmas produce chemical signals that only stimulate pollen tube growth from compatible pollen of the same species. This is a reproductive isolation mechanism that prevents hybridisation between different species. The pollen from Species A is not recognised by Species B's stigma, so the pollen tube does not grow and fertilisation cannot occur.
